In the 1970s, Daiei was Japan’s top retailer. But after Japan’s asset bubble burst around 1990, it became </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/326c9bc5-3d4f-4f91-bbb6-bfe26ce32d0b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Japan’s most famous “zombie” company</a><span> — staggering along unprofitably, kept afloat by a constant stream of below-market-rate loans from UFJ Bank and other big Japanese banks. Eventually the company was acquired by Aeon, a more successful retailer, and its once-storied brand is slated to be retired for good in the next few years. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I tend to be very skeptical of comparisons between post-1990 Japan and post-2021 China, because there are just so many differences between the two economies (and between the global economic environments at the time). Their industrial policies are different, their trading relationships are different, their bubbles and busts happened for very different reasons, and so on. But in the case of “zombie” companies, there may be some important parallels.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What’s important about Daiei is not how it failed, but </span><em>why it didn’t fail much sooner</em><span>. Caballero, Hoshi, and Kashyap </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bbc776a0-6e3a-4181-8a2b-d0509236e7c9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">wrote a paper in 2008</a><span> arguing that “zombie” companies like Daiei held the Japanese economy back during the 1990s (and, in some cases, even beyond the 1990s). </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The basic story is that after 1990, the Japanese economy slowed down, and lots of companies that used to be profitable — especially in the construction, retail, and trading sectors — were no longer profitable. These companies owed a lot of money to banks. If they stopped being able to pay back their loans, the banks would be forced to recognize </span><em>bad debt</em><span> on their books. This would get them in trouble with regulators (because of capital requirements), and it would also get them in trouble with the Japanese public. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So what the banks did was to lend </span><em>even more</em><span> money to the failing companies that already owed them a lot of money, at very cheap interest rates. The new loans were used to pay back the old loans, and the new loans would be classified on the bank’s books as “good” debt. This process — known as “evergreening” — kept banks from ever having to acknowledge their losses:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: Theoretically, the companies could have eventually pivoted their business models and recovered, or Japan’s economy could have started booming again, etc. In practice, this never happened.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Caballero, Hoshi, and Kashyap argue that evergreening was very bad for the Japanese economy, because it hoovered up scarce resources that better companies could have used to grow. With all of those crappy loans clogging up their books, Japanese banks couldn’t lend to healthier companies. With big zombies like Daiei still able to employ large amounts of Japan’s best managers, young scrappy upstarts were deprived of talent. The authors argue that keeping all of this labor and capital locked up inside doomed companies contributed significantly to Japan’s long productivity stagnation. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Why did the Japanese government allow this to happen? Preserving employment at the zombie companies was probably a big part of it. Japan had a strong tradition of job security at that point in time, and to throw so many people out of work — even if they could have gotten new jobs eventually — would have been seen as cruel and unfair. Social unrest was a possibility. Bank bailouts may also have been deeply politically unpopular. In any case, whatever the reason, throughout the 1990s the government supported banks with various capital injections and regulatory forbearance, without forcing banks to cut off the zombies.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Anyway, that’s Japan. The question is whether something like this will happen in China. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>China’s experience with its real estate bubble and bust doesn’t exactly parallel Japan’s, but there are some broad similarities. Since 2021, there has been a broad economic slowdown (probably </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cd74164b-85d2-4bf4-8ded-2eb2540e49ec?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">more severe</a><span> than the official numbers suggest), and a long-lasting chill in real-estate-related industries. This has predictably led to a rise in the number of loss-making companies:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure companies unable to pay their interest expenses, widespread suspicion that many of the companies whose loans are “performing” will never be able to repay those loans — matches the general pattern that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6360ec73-0632-4e89-b6fa-6db1a6f3c393?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Hoshi and Kashyap (2000)</a><span> documented in post-bubble Japan. Banks have taken a bunch of losses, but have refused to recognize those losses, using a flood of cheap debt to keep their borrowers afloat.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A bunch of people have warned about this. Here’s Rhodium:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Because of the political incentives shaping China’s financial system, banks in China tend to extend or roll over debt to poorly performing or loss-making companies. This can have some of the same effects as a subsidy, by removing incentives for companies to stay profitable and isolating them from market forces that would otherwise lead to their restructuring or bankruptcy….Evergreening of credit, therefore, allows firms to…[reduce] domestic and global prices to unprofitable levels[.]</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And here’s the Dallas Fed:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There is mounting evidence of “zombie lending” in China, banks rolling over bad loans to unprofitable firms and allowing the status quo to continue rather than recognize losses.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And here’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8bf5401e-9cee-4c66-b797-7edad1ef9ca7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a Business Times story</a><span> about how China’s government has allowed and even encouraged zombification, much as Japan did in the 1990s:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s impossible to quantify the true extent of the [bad debt] problem, though most economists say the ratio of bad loans is significantly higher than the 1.5 per cent official rate…One analyst at Absolute Strategy Research in London pegs it at about 10 per cent…Others say it could be double that amount…</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">While the [banks’] leniency [toward borrowers], largely condoned by regulators in Beijing, has helped maintain financial stability over the past few years, it also means the banking system is recycling capital into unproductive companies rather than spurring real growth in healthy firms…</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">[Government] officials have moved to bolster the nation’s six biggest banks with more than US$100 billion in fresh capital…[R]ather than cracking down on deadbeat borrowers, China’s banks are encouraged to cut them some slack. Regulators have for years urged the big banks to keep their reported bad loan ratio under 2 per cent, according to sources familiar with the guidance…As a result, banks routinely roll over maturing loans, extend repayment periods, or allow interest to be capitalised to avoid triggering NPL recognition.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now you might be tempted to think — and I’ve seen a few people argue — that this only matters in a </span><em>market </em><span>economy. In a market economy, undercapitalized banks matter because banks have to succeed or fail on their own. In a </span><em>state-directed </em><span>economy like China’s, the theory goes, debt on the banks’ books might as well be on the government’s books.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">¹</span><span> Banks can keep lending no matter how much bad debt they have, because the only entity that could punish them — the Chinese government — wants them to do so. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But while government control might avert a financial crisis, it doesn’t automatically solve the zombie problem, or make the comparison with Japan inappropriate.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First of all, it would be a mistake to see Japan’s government in the 1990s as operating at arm’s length from Japanese banks. It most certainly did not; in fact, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/767a03fe-aea8-45c9-bb25-a0c5f73c3f65?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">it acted to </a><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/767a03fe-aea8-45c9-bb25-a0c5f73c3f65?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">support </a></em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/767a03fe-aea8-45c9-bb25-a0c5f73c3f65?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the banks</a><span> that were supporting the zombies. The government bailed out the banks, deliberately turned a blind eye to the zombie problem, and encouraged banks to keep on lending to healthier companies despite the unrecognized bad loans on their books. That’s not </span><em>too </em><span>different from what China’s government </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/93fddd74-c6a0-4e52-9027-9eb876f782b8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">seems to have done</a><span> in response to the real estate bust, at least initially. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But simply having the government urge (or order) banks to keep lending didn’t solve the zombie problem in Japan, and it won’t solve it in China either. Even if the zombie companies don’t end up competing with healthier companies for </span><em>capital</em><span>, they compete with them for other resources. They compete for </span><em>labor </em><span>— workers who could be working at young, growing, healthy companies are instead being paid to continue to work for unproductive companies that are just spinning their wheels. They also compete for raw materials, for land, for energy, and so on. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">These resources are not in infinite supply, even in China. As long as unproductive zombie companies are hiring workers, hoovering up metals and chemicals and watts of electricity, and taking up prime real estate, they’re holding back the rest of the economy. This doesn’t just manifest as higher costs for healthy companies — it also shows up as increased competition. In 1990s Japan, if a new retailer wanted to enter the scene, it had to compete with Daiei, the unproductive behemoth that was essentially being paid by banks to produce below cost. The same will be true in China.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In fact, this may be a reason for the “involution” that Chinese companies are experiencing. In the wake of the real estate bust, China’s government directed banks to lend to manufacturing companies instead of to real estate-related companies. They did this (though some of the loans ended up sneaking back into the real estate sector). In fact, a large percent of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6af55a4e-3c92-4956-97ee-6e2b0e28648e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the “subsidies”</a><span> that China dishes out to its manufacturing companies is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5f9bd403-adcd-482d-8944-32145406ec06?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">through below-market-rate loans</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Some of these manufacturing companies will be successful and efficient — indeed, many already have been. But others are unproductive and inefficient. Instead of letting these die, China’s banks may keep them on as zombies as well, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dbc3ce0c-cb0d-4048-8066-8d48c4d690d6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">paying them to compete</a><span> with China’s healthier companies. Here’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2b3c4ad3-249d-4174-a67a-3167794e87d8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Alicia Garcia-Herrero</a><span> from back in March:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In many sectors, including…electric vehicles, solar panels, batteries, and other green technologies…Chinese firms…keep selling at rock-bottom levels, sometimes below what it costs to produce, just to hold onto market share. A growing number of these companies cannot earn enough revenue to even service their debt…These “zombie” companies survive only because banks roll over loans and local governments provide subsidies to avoid job losses and keep tax revenues flowing…In newer, high-priority sectors like green tech, the share of zombie companies has hit 30 percent of total listed companies…</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Without real productivity advances, [zombies] still join the price-slashing frenzy to stay in the game thanks to external support from banks or local governments. They cut prices aggressively…The outcome is predictable: collapsing profit margins across the board, even for the better companies, whose productivity is increasing.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When we Westerners think about the effect of Chinese zombification, we often think about </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/28022480-ff87-46c9-8eab-8efa72170ad2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the flood of cheap exports</a><span> threatening to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a31ee9c9-4dc5-4647-9483-6cf8d929634a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">deindustrialize Europe </a><span>and other regions. But while that export dominance might seem like a victory to China’s mercantilist leaders, it’s a double-edged sword, because zombification reduces productivity at home. In the long run, lower productivity hurts growth, despite the temporary bump from exports.  </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In other words, China’s fusion between the financial system and the state may have made zombification </span><em>worse</em><span>, not better. The Chinese state is not a ruthlessly efficient allocator of capital; it has sociopolitical goals just like any other state, and it fears the unrest that could result from widespread corporate failure and unemployment. Yes, it can tell banks to lend to manufacturers instead of property developers, but that just ends up adding </span><em>more </em><span>zombies to the horde.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And at some point, even state-owned and state-directed banks probably do care about profitability. Yes, the government can bail out any bank at will, but if you’re the bank executive or manager who dished out the bad loans and made a bailout necessary, your career might be over. This might be why corporate loans have started to fall slightly from the torrid pace of 2023-24:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Many people have compared our current era to the Gilded Age. But that analogy is deeply unfair to the Gilded Age. Like the robber barons of yore, today’s oligarchs are immensely wealthy — even wealthier, relative to the economy as a whole, than their predecessors. And extreme wealth corrupts our democracy. But the corruption is deeper and more destructive now than it was then: The mitigating factors that once put some brakes on the harm done by excessive wealth concentration are now mostly gone.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>About wealth concentration: The standard source for information on extreme wealth is the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4349c835-6add-4eaa-83fc-dba89d7ad045?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Forbes 400 list</a><span>. Forbes only began compiling that list in its current form in 1982, but it published its first listing of America’s top fortunes in 1918. The chart above compares the wealth of the richest 5 Americans in 1918 with that of the richest 15 in 2025 — 15, not 5, because the total U.S. population more than tripled over that period. I scale their wealth both as a percentage of total wealth and as a share of GDP.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Either way, the concentration of wealth at the very top is much higher now than it ever was during the Gilded Age. And these are numbers from last year, before the SpaceX IPO. The robber barons were pikers compared with today’s oligarchs.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This level of wealth brings with it immense political influence. A </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1c9f6eaa-f1e1-4260-b4e5-f60fdb38da6c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">New York Times analysis</a><span> found that 300 billionaires accounted for 19 percent of political contributions in the 2024 election. And since the election the power of money has grown even stronger.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In part this reflects the way great wealth has been used to corrupt the media. Elon Musk bought Twitter, not as a financial investment, but to turn it into the right-wing fever swamp it has now become. Larry Ellison, America’s second-richest man, purchased CBS basically to destroy it as an independent news source and convert it into Fox News 2.0, a goal he is achieving — and he is now on track to do the same to CNN.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On top of this, the presidency is now more or less openly for sale. “Donald Trump,” writes </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7be5755b-ee9a-4a0b-9194-dbcea98fcf38?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Forbes</a><span>, “has presided over the most lucrative presidency in history,” adding $4.2 billion to his personal wealth since regaining the White House.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There were many corruption scandals during the Gilded Age, but none on this scale.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What do today’s uberrich do with their political power? Much of what they push for involves their own self-interest. In 2024 Mark Zuckerberg basically used his financial clout to kill </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0ebcc8c5-423f-4ca0-b1a0-45c1fd65aca0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">bipartisan legislation</a><span> that would have tried to protect children from psychological harm due to social media and, of course, put some restrictions on Meta. The Koch family has spent decades doing everything it can to prevent action against climate change and keep America burning fossil fuels.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Beyond this, some megabillionaires use their power to push political extremism.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>True, Elon Musk is something of an outlier; you have to go some ways down the list to find someone comparably extreme (Peter Thiel is #40.) And he isn’t the first incredibly wealthy man to be deeply bigoted and an avid consumer of conspiracy theories: Henry Ford was a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6a55cf90-16ad-413a-becb-643c04e215aa?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">rabid anti-Semite</a><span> who published and distributed </span><em>The Protocols of the Elders of Zion</em><span>, a forgery probably concocted by the Russian secret police.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Still, it’s remarkable that the world’s richest man has passionately embraced the “Great Replacement” theory of a sinister conspiracy to replace whites with nonwhite immigrants.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And it’s equally remarkable that our political system accepts it as a fact of life that such a person should command such power, even leaving on one side the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5e915d4e-60cb-4daa-8bd5-3e92cbe42b87?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">dubious roots</a><span> of his wealth. Where’s the outrage?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Obviously some Americans </span><em>are</em><span> outraged, but the backlash against a highly corrupt, rigged system is far weaker than one might have expected. Why?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’ll return to this question in later posts, but it’s clear that modern America suffers from a combination of cynicism — “everybody does it” — and fatalism — “that’s just how the world works” — far worse than anything we experienced in the robber baron era.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">You can see this moral malaise in the shrugs with which all too many politicians, especially but not only Republicans, greet each new revelation of presidential scandal. You can also see it in the behavior of the ultrawealthy themselves.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Make no mistake: the men on that 1918 Forbes list were, without exception, ruthless businessmen. The term “robber barons,” popularized in the 1930s by the historian Mattew Josephson, was apt. The great fortunes of the late 19</span><sup style="font-size: 0.75em;line-height: 0;">th</sup><span> and early 20</span><sup style="font-size: 0.75em;line-height: 0;">th</sup><span> centuries were accumulated by men who functionally played the same role as feudal warlords extorting tolls from travelers passing their castles. In particular, John D. Rockefeller, the world’s richest man, in effect controlled an essential economic choke point, a sort of financial Strait of Hormuz, through his monopolization of oil refining.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Yet many of the robber barons also possessed a sense of noblesse oblige, believing that they should deploy some of their riches on behalf of the public good.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Many of the robber barons gave </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ec8f0f7d-46eb-4f00-a7cd-1c3e06781cb1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">huge sums to philanthropy</a><span>. These included large donations to cultural institutions, which continue to enrich our society to this day. Mention Andrew Carnegie or Henry Clay Frick to a modern New Yorker and the first things they think of will probably be Carnegie Hall and the Frick Collection of fine art.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">No doubt this was in large part a public relations exercise, but the fact that the robber barons believed that this PR effort was necessary was itself a symptom of a society less cynical than it is today. And the Gilded Age wealthy left a lasting legacy of good deeds to set against the history of their ruthless business practices.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>By contrast, today’s oligarchs spend very little on good works, according to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b575c476-43cb-4993-a0ef-069b7ea47070?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Forbes</a><span>. Musk and Ellison have both given away less than 1 percent of their fortunes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And Musk in particular is the opposite of a philanthropist. Not only doesn’t he spend any of his own money to help others, he used his power when running DOGE to cut off aid to poor countries, condemning hundreds of thousands of children to avoidable death. And he was gleeful about it:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table Of course, those people are all more pro-Israel than I am. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But there’s also a rogue doctrine out there that I’m going to call the Positive Good theory of Platnerism. href="https://substack.com/redirect/6da3a401-6093-4b3a-beb8-a2de25894b86?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">apparent womanizing</a><span> are forgivable or unimportant, but that these qualities actually make him an above-average Democrat. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ken Klippenstein </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7b1be8a2-90df-436b-80e7-0021020f9b71?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" href="https://substack.com/redirect/297dc3d2-90bf-45c8-9b3c-2379313a24c0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">lengthy quasi-apology for the sexist joke</a><span> paired with a detailed sociological theory of the rise and nature of American H.R. practices that bears no relationship whatsoever to any policy analysis that Platner has ever offered. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I think this Positive Good Platnerism is preposterous, but it’s in the neighborhood of something correct and insightful. </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s not just that Democrats in general ought to be more moderate on cultural issues.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s that in particular</span><em>,</em><span> people who want Democrats to advance a more left-wing economic agenda need </span><em>even more</em><span> moderation on culture than those of us willing to advocate for across-the-board moderation. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The problem is that guys like Stoller and Klippenstein don’t want to call for moderation on concrete cultural issues. So they’re left instead with the preposterous idea that instead of nominees who just have more chill stances on policy questions, what Democrats really need are nominees whose personal conduct is inconsistent with their stated values. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The needed disclaimer about Maine</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I feel like I’ve said this a half dozen times already, but the cursed thing about all Platner Discourse is that the broad center-left community desperately </span><em>wants</em><span> to have an argument about what kind of candidate can win back working-class Obama-Trump crossover voters in red states, but instead we’re stuck arguing about a guy who’s running in Maine. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Maine is a state that Kamala Harris </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8a479538-152a-466c-a4cd-67dd5bc5b862?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">won 52.4 to 45.5</a><span> in a bad political climate for Democrats nationally. In the Silver Bulletin’s generic ballot model, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2418cc46-d0c4-4d7a-b352-2f5d1dca87a8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Maine is currently a D+14 state</a><span>. Lakshya Jain’s model for The Argument is even more bullish and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5def51f0-89fe-4ef8-8a21-0981eb1a1248?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">sees a D+16 edge</a><span>. I’ve been really mad at progressives for running Jared Golden out of Congress because I was pretty sure they were giving away his fairly red House seat to the Republican Party. But if you take those numbers seriously, a pretty generic Dem should be able to win the Second Congressional District this year. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Platner has a challenging race on his hands, but that’s just because Susan Collins is a very strong electoral performer who has won races even when the national environment favored Democrats. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is an interesting political challenge, but it’s not one that has any broader implications for political strategy because there are literally no other Republicans holding down Senate seats in states that Harris won. The whole task here is just to get people who voted for Harris to vote for Platner. Obviously if some disgruntled Trump voters want to vote for him too, that would be great. But there’s no evidence he’s going to pull that off and also no need for him to pull it off. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s true that the part of Maine that Platner is from (the part of the state where I spend my summers) is very rural, but it’s also quite liberal. Harris got </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/39beb7f4-db89-41ca-bc76-8426e954e7ee?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">55 percent of the vote</a><span> in Hancock County. Platner held a big rally with Ro Khanna in Bar Harbor, which is an upscale resort town. His victory rally was at the Y.M.C.A. in Blue Hill, which is the kind of small town that has a food co-op and two yoga studios and an economy based primarily on summer residents and cute B&Bs. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To be clear, there is nothing wrong with any of this. He is not running in Alaska like Mary Peltola or Texas like James Talarico or Ohio like Sherrod Brown or even North Carolina like Roy Cooper. He doesn’t need to reach out to Trump voters, he doesn’t need to expand the tent, and I think he’s probably going to win because he’s a pretty charismatic guy who has the macro winds of politics at his back. But for the purposes of understanding the Platner meta-discourse, you have to ignore reality and </span><em>pretend</em><span> that this race is a good proxy for rival theories about how to expand the Democratic Party. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Democrats’ actual problem</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Democratic Party is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6cf51714-6c5b-423e-8884-56db0f1d141b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">seen by many people</a><span> as weird, extreme, and hostile to their basic moral values and interests. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Many believe that Democrats practice discrimination against white people, that they prioritize the interests of environmentalists and labor unions over economic growth, that they’ve embraced bizarre ideas about gender identity, that they care more about criminals and illegal immigrants than about law-abiding Americans. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Republicans, fortunately for Democrats, have their own set of vulnerabilities. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But the people who are voting repeatedly for Donald Trump are clearly people who have a big problem with Democrats. Trump himself has never been particularly popular. For all the attention lavished on Trump’s base who’ll forgive him anything, it’s not like he puts up overwhelming numbers in his election wins. Instead, there are plenty of marginal voters out there who see very real flaws in Trump but just think Democrats are worse. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The problem, in other words, is that too many people disagree with some of Democrats’ high-profile issue positions. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Peltola and Talarico are trying to address this by having different issue positions, especially on their home states’ natural resource economies. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Platner, to his credit, also has one issue like this — guns — where he argues that national Democrats’ enthusiasm for banning assault weapons is unresponsive to real crime problems and disrespectful of law-abiding gun enthusiasts’ hobbies. That’s not the issue that I would pick, but it does seem to be authentic to his life and interests, so good for him. I support a big tent. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the idea that you could take a baseline Democrat and have him overperform in North Carolina not by being more moderate on policy issues, but by cheating on his wife and therefore proving he’s not a “smoothgroin” is ridiculous. We literally ran this experiment with Cal Cunningham and it went </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/975d9cac-9cc1-495c-af27-e4338ffee405?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">as you’d expect</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you want to reject “H.R. lady politics” by rejecting D.E.I. initiatives or the way the Biden administration handled sexual assault allegations on campus or by proposing child care initiatives that are attentive to the interests of stay-at-home moms, that’s great (though, personally, I would try to come up with a non-misogynistic way to characterize these ideas). </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But Platner hasn’t done any of those things. He’s just made some off-color remarks in Reddit posts and maybe fibbed about a tattoo while adhering to orthodox progressive views. That doesn’t make any sense as a theory of change. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And the vast majority of Democrats can see, I think, that it doesn’t make sense. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The problem is that while 80 percent of the party disagrees with Stoller and Klippenstein, the party itself is trafficking in a low-effort version of the same politics. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is the idea that if you put up a white man with good hair like Gavin Newsom or find the perfect tattooed veteran with a gruff voice, that will somehow pull the wool over voters’ eyes and they’ll forget about their substantive disagreements with progressive politics. </p><div class="subscribe-widget is-signed-up is-fully-subscribed" data-component-name="SubscribeWidget" style="margin: 0 0 1em;direction: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Platner needs to normalize his campaign</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Again, though, </span><em>Platner</em><span> doesn’t actually need to win over anyone who is profoundly alienated from the Democratic Party. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The thing he needs to do is to distinguish more clearly between the interests of his campaign and the interests of factionalists who want to leverage his campaign to advance their own careers and agendas. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The best part of his primary victory speech was when he thanked Janet Mills for a lifetime of service to the people of Maine. Not because it was a brilliant piece of rhetoric or anything, but just because it was classy and normal and conveyed to people who believed in good faith that she would have been the better nominee that he likes and respects them and wants them to vote for him. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Platner and other leftists backed Troy Jackson for governor. Maine’s ranked-choice counting is very slow, but Jackson </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/21e98139-d0a3-43c9-8cfe-05448ac0c620?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">seems extremely unlikely to prevail</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In a way, I think that’s good for Platner. Democrats will have a gubernatorial nominee who Platner didn’t endorse and the two of them can appear together at a unity rally and invite Chellie Pingree and whoever else to speak and all talk about how it’s important to stop the MAGA movement. Interesting intra-party factionalism is what brought Platner this far, and it might be good enough to win in November. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But clearly his optimal strategy is to be Mr. Normie Dem who everyone’s going to vote for because he won’t confirm MAGA judges and will re-instate the health-insurance tax credits that Republicans allowed to lapse. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">You often see people committing what I’ve called “the pundit’s fallacy,” where they insist that the way to win swing voters is to just say things the writer agrees with. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I often get accused of this, but it’s sincerely not what I think. I want to see Democrats run pro-life candidates in the South not because I’m pro-life, but because voters in the South are. I’ve been a huge proponent of Josh Turek’s campaign, but I would never in a million years suggest that he </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6ce0615a-5216-42fa-84eb-fb5fb4214261?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">agree with me about biofuels</a><span>. It’s politics. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But in the specific context of the Maine Senate race, the relevant swing voters really are people like me: Democrats who do not particularly welcome the ascendancy of the Bernie factionalists but who think Donald Trump is worse. </p><p class="button-wrapper" Trump celebrated his 80</span><sup style="font-size: 0.75em;line-height: 0;">th</sup><span> birthday with a cage match on the White House lawn. The match and the events that surrounded it — especially the press conference with UFC fighters, shown above, held on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial — were a desecration of America’s capital, whose monuments and buildings have always endeavored to represent small-r republican virtues. The whole affair was an affront to the values on which this nation was founded and also unspeakably vulgar.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That last criticism may strike some readers as elitist and trivial. Yet the vulgarity that is the hallmark of Trump and his surrounding circle of oligarchs is a symptom of something not at all trivial: The collapse of social norms. As I argued </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/59b2c770-83ff-445a-9a84-b2ba113ab893?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">yesterday</a><span>, these norms historically played a key role in mitigating abuses of power and privilege during the Gilded Age, the last time America suffered from extreme income and wealth inequality (though not nearly as extreme as what we have now).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Norms matter. In his classic book </span><em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aedc7a4e-1dde-458f-9cab-6e1fd9a8a820?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Theory of the Leisure Class</a></em><span> — published in 1899, at the apogee of the Gilded Age — Thorstein Veblen famously argued that much of the behavior of his era’s elite was driven not by the desire to enjoy life but by the desire to impress others. Partly they did this through conspicuous consumption. Thus they built lavish mansions staffed by legions of servants.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, members of the Gilded Age elite didn’t solely aim to display their wealth. They also tried to appear respectable. There were surely many private affairs and betrayals we will never know about. But the important point is that the super-wealthy of that era presented to the American public an </span><a upstanding behavior, the extremely rich of the Gilded Age were expected to have, or pretend to have, some virtues that were part of the aristocratic ideal, including a sense of noblesse oblige displayed by good works. Veblen was quite cynical about philanthropy, yet even he didn’t dismiss it completely, stating that:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The fact itself that distinction or a decent good fame is sought by this method [such as the endowment of a university, public library or museum] is evidence of a prevalent sense of the legitimacy, and of the presumptive effectual presence, of a non-emulative, non-invidious interest, as a consistent factor in the habits of thought of modern communities.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">(Veblen’s lasting intellectual influence did not come from his sparkling prose style.)</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Today’s oligarchs, by contrast, have largely given up on the old norms of social and individual responsibility. They give very little money to good causes and their vulgar taste reflects their in-your-face attitude towards the public. In our current hyper-Gilded Age, extreme vulgarity and the decline of philanthropy are really different aspects of the same phenomenon: the rise of an elite so disconnected from ordinary Americans that it feels no need to even appear to be honorable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So in a real sense we are living in the midst of a reenactment of the decline and fall of the Roman Republic, not a second American Gilded Age. No, I’m not one of those men who </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/834114f0-6ca4-4021-80f4-0153fc5aba0b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">thinks about ancient Rome</a><span> all the time. But there are some obvious parallels.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">While the causes of the decline of republican government and Rome’s eventual transition to one-man rule were doubtless complex, there is broad consensus among historians that a key factor was the emergence of extreme inequality. A handful of men became incredibly wealthy from the spoils of Rome’s eastern conquests, and their wealth and power eventually became too great for the rules of constitutional, republican government to contain. Sound uncomfortably familiar?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4b5db6da-c978-439f-9f5f-a43cd1112f96?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">death throes of the Republic</a><span> went on for many years. Politicians declared their rivals enemies of the state, deployed violent gangs to disrupt the rule of law, established temporary dictatorships, and more. The installation of Augustus as emperor in 27 BC was just the final act.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And during this long twilight of constitutional government, one of the ways the extremely wealthy and powerful sought both to demonstrate their wealth and to curry favor with the mob was by sponsoring </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2511e52d-59fb-4d73-be3a-6dd1c46194f9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">gladiatorial games</a><span>:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1280" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/af230fbc-181c-4cec-ae57-683506630ac1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/77cb0e56-8ff0-4281-ad12-1171681ddbd7_1280x853.jpeg","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":853,"width":1280,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":"See Who Attended Trump's UFC Cage Fight on the White House Lawn - like to see us thinking about immigration. Don’t identify flaws in our visa programs and use those flaws as an argument for cutting them. Identify flaws and fix them! And since you’re making immigration better, why not have more of it?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The basic story here is that skilled immigration in particular pays a kind of double dividend in terms of debt sustainability. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The United States has a progressive tax system, and a very large share of our spending is on retired people and national defense. A new worker with an above-average income pays a lot of taxes without increasing our spending burdens in the short term. Meanwhile, immigrants are also growing the denominator of the debt-to-G.D.P. ratio. A large country like Germany can sustain more debt than a small country like Portugal. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">You can’t just pursue population growth as an alternative to responsible budgeting, because eventually your spending commitments will catch up to you. But even though “just kicking the can down the road” is easy to deride, it’s actually useful. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Making small changes to Social Security like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1911cfc0-5841-4f3c-9ad8-48066cbd1356?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">adding an employer compensation tax</a><span> could strengthen the program without fully saving it. But if you manage to extend the timeline with immigration, then those smaller tweaks have more time to work. It’s both/and, not either/or. I also know a lot of smart people who think all these fiscal issues will be obsolete soon thanks to artificial intelligence delivering a post-scarcity society. I don’t think it’s smart to count on that, but however far we manage to kick the can down the road, we raise the odds of being rescued by something like that. </span></p><div class="subscribe-widget 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Temporary migration for fiscal benefit</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You could do a lot more than Manhattan proposes to maximize the fiscal upside of immigration, though. Right now, H-2A seasonal agricultural workers </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aa11c94c-4199-43d0-89f8-db146607ac7d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">are exempt from payroll taxes</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is theoretically part of the contributory structure of Social Security and Medicare. Temporary agricultural workers are not eligible to receive benefits from these programs, so they don’t need to pay into the funds that support them. That seems a little bit weirdly literal. The whole deal with taxes is that while it’s useful to have revenue, people also prefer not to pay taxes. But if H-2A workers needed to contribute payroll taxes, there would still be plenty of people who wanted the visas. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If anything, I’d consider tacking an extra one percentage point on to both sides of temporary workers’ payroll taxes. The extra bit that the employers kick in could be a “solidarity fee” for American workers, and the extra bit that workers pay could be handed over when they leave the country on schedule with a record of good conduct. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Of course, farm employers wouldn’t like any of this because it would raise their labor costs. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the point here is that if you make immigrant labor more clearly beneficial to the American people as a whole, then you have a strong case for issuing more H-2A visas or making them easier to get. This would also become a model for expanding temporary work. Dairy farmers are always complaining that they </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f77a5b35-fab3-4af8-9e8d-429a0923cd72?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">want access to agricultural guest workers</a><span> but are currently ineligible because dairy work isn’t seasonal. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I don’t know exactly how far we’d ultimately want to push this model where low-skill workers come to work in the United States for nine-to-18 months and then go home, having contributed payroll taxes without becoming eligible for Social Security and Medicare. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But during times of labor market tightness, relying on workers like that — vetted, legally authorized ones who are making a defined fiscal contribution to the United States — seems a lot better than the kinds of ad hoc parole programs the Biden administration tried to use. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In general, it makes sense to me that one of the best ways to deter illegal migration and total chaos is to create legal channels to meet demand for labor. But even though doing it through backdoor executive action is easier than working with Congress to change laws (almost everything is easier than getting Congress to change laws), legislation is required to really unlock the big upsides. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The flywheel of growth</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There are, of course, other issues. The United States is short on housing at the moment, and even if an increase in immigrant flows has fiscal benefits, it could exacerbate that shortage. We also have big issues with our electricity grid. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But while I hear all the time from rightists who argue that restricting immigration, rather than pursuing land use reform, is the real solution to housing issues, I think that’s pretty terrible loser behavior. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Certainly I don’t see any of the people arguing for immigration restrictions pushing for big tax increases to solve the budget deficit. And the politics of a Paul Ryan-style push for an all-cuts approach is absolutely horrible. Donald Trump’s only really good political move was getting Republicans off that idea. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But you’ve got to do something. </p><p class="button-wrapper" continues to be a relatively sparsely populated country with abundant natural resources and the privilege of being a place where huge numbers of people would like to live. We should be selective about the people we invite to be permanent residents, but when you can recruit people of above-average ability and decent values to come to your country, it’s a good idea to do that. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We can also use the tax code to ensure temporary labor is advantageous to the American people as a whole. Building more housing to accommodate more people is not a difficult engineering problem. In the relatively recent past, small American towns became booming cities surrounded by extensive suburbs. optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Lessons, implications, and silver linings from the Iran War</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Beyond the direct fallout from Iran’s victory, and the simple lesson that Trump and his administration are grossly incompetent, I think there are a number of things we can learn — or at least begin to suspect — from the Iran War. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The big lesson, I think, is that the revolution in military affairs is real. An “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0c8261e0-9673-4ef5-a7c6-e6725f8357b4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">RMA</a><span>”, as they call it, is when battlefield technology changes so much that it forces a change in the way wars are fought. The advent of gunpowder reduced the role of cavalry and forced wars to be far more slow-moving and positional. The advent of combustion engines allowed tanks and planes to flow around or blast through defenses. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now the age of cheap precision weaponry has changed the game again. 26px;font-size: 16px;">Iran proved this yet again on the battlefield. It didn’t use masses of FPV drones to destroy American ground forces, as Ukraine is doing to Russia. Instead it used long-range strike drones and drone boats to effect a naval blockade. But many of the fundamental strengths of drone warfare were still on display. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Drones are </span><strong>relatively easy to make</strong><span>, which is one reason Iran was able to preserve so much of its defense industry from American strikes. They’re </span><strong>cheap and numerous</strong><span> and </span><strong>can be launched from almost anywhere</strong><span>, which is a major reason the U.S. was unable to suppress Iran’s fire. And their low price tag meant that the U.S., with its reliance on expensive missiles and planes and ships, was paying far more to fight the war than Iran was.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The advent of cheap precision weaponry means that what constitutes a “superpower” is not as clear as in the past. The wars in Iran and Ukraine both demonstrate that with cheap drones, middle powers can hold off great powers. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a0ea7e58-ec8c-4e72-94b1-a48a11bade4e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Yaroslav Trofimov writes</a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Great powers, it turns out, don’t have as much power as they thought…[T]echnological advances—such as drones and much cheaper precision missiles—have leveled the playing field between the smaller states and the great powers that are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on their armed forces…Regime change—Russia’s goal in Ukraine, and, initially at least, America’s in Iran—can no longer be achieved just by the force of arms in the modern world…</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The swift removal of Venezuela’s strongman Nicolás Maduro in January—which seemed at the time like a precursor of things to come, whetting Trump’s appetite for Greenland and Iran—now appears as a rare exception rather than a harbinger of the future exercise of American might.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Trofimov surmises that a Chinese invasion of Taiwan might be similarly thwarted, and he might be right. But this comes with an asterisk when it comes to Chinese power. China, with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/849fe23a-78bc-4cf9-8b81-b4106018d06f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">its mastery of the electric tech stack</a><span>, is the place where almost all of the drone components come from — batteries, magnets, and motors. Ukraine and Iran were able to resist because they could import components from China. Taiwan probably wouldn’t be able to do the same.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So because of China’s might in electric technology, it’s not clear yet whether the lesson is that all great powers are weak, or merely that “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6e9590d0-1a4c-4a9c-9e29-50496fa78126?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">aerospace republics</a><span>” like the U.S. and Russia, whose economies are based around 20th century combustion industries, are unable to fight modern wars.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But one silver lining of the Iran War is that now much of the U.S. — the Pentagon, the pundit class, and the military itself — realize that the revolution in military affairs is real. Before the war, there was a ton of inertia and resistance to the idea that drones had changed the game of war — now, after a lost war, the necessary scramble to retool the U.S. military and the U.S. defense-industrial base around drones and electric technology might finally begin in earnest. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>America has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cba1a2b8-ee06-4cd1-b130-c8d2059c18aa?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">fast-tracked its own cheap strike drone</a><span>, and is throwing a large amount of money at </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/42f907a6-7adb-4904-8501-039786bb8e33?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">counter-drone capabilities</a><span> — two efforts that were in progress before the war, but are now probably being sped up because of it. These aren’t nearly enough, but they’re a start.  </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There are other potential silver linings as well. First, the spike in oil prices will probably accelerate the world’s transition away from fossil fuels. Climate change itself was insufficient to motivate countries to go all-in on solar and batteries, but Iran’s newfound control over Hormuz will provide a stronger push. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Recall that the transition toward fuel-efficient vehicles in the 70s and early 80s — and the increased research into solar power that ultimately made the technology competitive — was in response to the 1973 and 1979 oil shocks. The impact of the Iran War may be similar — with the exception that this time, there’s an energy technology that’s actually </span><em>cheaper </em><span>than fossil fuels in most cases. That will allow countries to transition away from oil without suffering the kind of economic damage that they suffered in the 70s. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A final silver lining is that the U.S. may step back from the Middle East in general, as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a9b92ad0-df1d-4fdb-a1d7-6c65695b21d0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">I’ve long been urging</a><span>. This includes stepping back from the alliance with Israel, which has proven itself to be the unreliable ally that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f1c0fb03-f9cd-470c-bcfc-cb56d300273c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">I’ve long alleged</a><span>. It would be wrong to entirely blame Israel’s Prime Minister Netanyahu for dragging Trump into the disastrous Iran War, but it’s undeniable that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/df1c79c9-0630-4d59-88ca-0b9de0373766?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">he helped convince Trump to take the leap</a><span>. More generally, Israel will probably not stop fighting with Iran, and the U.S. has very little interest in continuing to fight with Iran. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I don’t see the U.S. breaking off its alliance with Israel anytime soon, but I see America washing its hands of Israel’s conflicts and potentially dialing back military aid. This will be upsetting for supporters of the alliance, but ultimately it will be healthy for the U.S., which will find it easier to pivot to far more important theaters in Asia and Europe.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In other words, Trump lost a war and proved himself and his administration to be grossly incompetent. It provides a strong reason to return Democrats to power, and to select more intelligent conservatives within the GOP. But it was ultimately a relatively cheap defeat, and one that may lead to needed pivots and realizations. Iran’s regime is an evil one, but hopefully by defeating the mighty United States and its fool of a President, it will push us to make changes that were long in coming. </p><div style="font-size: style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>Brief post today on amazing things happening in the markets.</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">While I don’t know anyone who loves Microsoft or its products, it’s a wildly successful company with a long track record. Last year Microsoft earned $125 billion in profits on $318 billion in revenue.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In that same year SpaceX lost $4 billion on $19 billion in revenue. Robin Wigglesworth, editor of the </span><em>Financial Times </em><span>blog </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/35574a5c-efc1-43c4-bd34-5ec964285c00?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Alphaville</a><span>, memorably </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/874bccda-2fdc-48ee-b906-4828789d536f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">described</a><span> Elon Musk’s company as a</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">very successful but fairly small satellite launch company, bolted onto a stagnant money-losing social media company [X, formerly Twitter] and a money-incinerating AI company [xAI, operator of the widely despised model Grok], and then sprinkled with a lot of hype about humankind going interplanetary.</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And yet at the end of trading yesterday the stock market placed almost as high a value on SpaceX, which went public last Friday, as it did on Microsoft, and slightly more than it placed on Amazon, which made $78 billion in profits last year.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What can explain this valuation? Many investors appear to believe that Musk is a wizard who can conjure up world-conquering inventions on a regular basis. But while Musk has done some impressive things, his track record for more than a decade has been one of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c6cb83fa-4880-45cd-b7cb-124111a82c05?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">failed venture after failed venture</a><span>. And his current big ideas, like data centers in space, fundamentally don’t make sense. A recent </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/21511ad6-2e61-4316-a390-9ad3c46f896f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Government Accountability Office</a><span> report is carefully worded, but as I read it basically says “this is another Hyperloop [Musk’s absurd, failed attempt to reinvent public transportation].”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Granted, Musk has enormous political influence through his close ties to Donald Trump. So might SpaceX’s valuation be justified, not by Musk’s technological prowess, but by his access to the fruits of crony capitalism?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Nobody should doubt the Trump administration’s willingness to tilt the playing field in favor of its friends, especially those who enrich Trump personally. But there are limits to what even blatant favoritism can deliver.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider the current fate of the crypto industry. Trump, who once called Bitcoin a “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/816a915a-a934-43f7-9f34-b6e5922d0ec4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">scam</a><span>,” became a passionate booster of cryptocurrency once it became clear that it was a channel through which he could profit from the presidency. The fighting cage he had erected on the White House lawn was “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d4b3823b-9d50-4267-a869-d7c1c235f735?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">wrapped in cryptocurrency advertisements</a><span>.” And cryptocurrency valuations soared after he won in 2024.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But the Trump bump for crypto has now vanished. Here’s the total market capitalization of Bitcoin over the past two and a half years:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px
